title: The Adventure (Hornbill)
tagline: Jayant Narlikar’s professor of history wakes in an India where the Marathas won Panipat — and has to prove it.

overview.intro: A science-fiction story set not in space but in time. Professor Gangadharpant Gaitonde, a historian, finds himself in a world where the Third Battle of Panipat went the other way and the Marathas won; in that world India’s history, cities and rulers follow a different line. The unit follows his journey through that alternate present, the evidence he gathers, the lecture at which he is ejected, and Rajendra Deshpande’s scientific account of how two histories could both be real.

learn.title: Two histories: waking in the other India

blocks.text: The story’s premise is delivered through detail rather than explanation. Gangadharpant, a historian who has spent his life studying the Maratha defeat at Panipat, finds that the world around him has shifted: the landscape outside his train window, the city he arrives in, and the institutions he walks through belong to an India in which the Battle of Panipat was won by the Marathas. Vishwasrao, whose death in the real battle broke the Maratha army, survived in this version, and from that single non-event a different political order follows — one in which the pattern of foreign dominance that the student of Indian history knows never took its familiar course.

The story’s method is to state the altered facts calmly. Buildings, streets and civic arrangements are described as normal by the people who live in them and as astonishing only to the reader’s guest, and that gap — between the ordinary and the counterfactual — is the pleasure of the premise. Gangadharpant’s professional knowledge is what makes the difference legible: a layman would see a different city, but a historian sees the whole chain of consequences that followed from one battle, which is why the protagonist must be the expert he is.

learn.title: The investigation: the lecture, the chair and the torn page

blocks.text: The professor does not simply observe; he tests. In the alternate city he attends a public lecture at a meeting where the presidential chair has not been provided — a detail that matters because in his own world such a meeting has its protocols — and when he tries to occupy the place a president would take, the crowd turns on him and ejects him. The scene is comic and pointed at once: his claim to the chair is a claim to standing in that society, and the society rejects it because his version of history has no authority there.

The documentary evidence is the torn page. Consulting a history book of that world, he finds the account of the battle with a page missing — the missing leaf being the one that would have explained how events there diverged from the record he knows. The torn page is the story’s clue in the classic detective sense: an absence that proves the alteration, and the moment where the fantastic premise acquires something solid enough to argue about. The two pieces of evidence — the rejected chair and the missing page — summarise the professor’s situation: in that world his knowledge has no seat and his truth has no page.

learn.title: Rajendra Deshpande’s explanation: catastrophe and quantum ideas

blocks.text: The story belongs to the genre that explains rather than merely astonishes, and its explanation comes from Rajendra Deshpande, the professor’s friend. Two scientific ideas frame his account. The first is catastrophe theory: systems can move from one stable state to another across a threshold, so that a single small event at a critical moment — a battle, a death — can tip a whole arrangement of things into a different configuration. The second draws on quantum ideas about the behaviour of physical systems at the smallest scale, where outcomes are not single until they occur, and the story uses these as imaginative licence to suggest that histories themselves might branch rather than proceed in one line.

The conversation between the two men is the story’s real climax, and its design is deliberate: the fantastic journey has prepared the reader to accept a discussion of history and physics that would otherwise be dry. Deshpande’s account also reframes the professor’s adventure — what felt like a dream becomes a hypothesis, and the torn page becomes data. Examination answers should present the science as the story presents it: as a plausible-sounding framework offered within fiction, not as established physics, because the text’s interest is in the question of what makes history inevitable rather than in the mechanics of time travel.

learn.title: History, contingency and what the story is arguing

blocks.text: Beneath the science fiction the story poses an old historical question: how contingent is the past? By changing one battle’s outcome and following the consequences through cities and institutions, Narlikar dramatises the claim that history is not a single inevitable road but a series of outcomes that might have gone otherwise. The Maratha defeat at Panipat is one of the great hinge-events of eighteenth-century India, which makes it an ideal choice: no serious reader of Indian history can treat it as the only possible result.

The story also makes a subtler point through its protagonist. Gangadharpant is not a hero who changes the alternate world; he is an observer who cannot be believed in it — ejected from a meeting, unable to lodge his version of events anywhere. The lesson is about knowledge itself: each history produces its own experts, its own documents and its own chairs, and a fact that has no page in the book cannot claim authority. For long answers, this is the line to develop, because it unites the plot’s comedy (the chair), its clue (the torn page) and its science (Deshpande’s explanation) into a single argument about how pasts are recorded and believed.

questions.prompt: What does Professor Gaitonde discover in the world he wakes in?
questions.answer: He discovers an India whose history did not run the way his own study says it did: the Third Battle of Panipat was won by the Marathas instead of lost, Vishwasrao did not die, and the political order that followed the recorded defeat — including the pattern of foreign dominance he has spent his life studying — never took shape. The cities, institutions and arrangements he walks through are ordinary to their inhabitants, and it is only his specialist knowledge that lets him read how one altered battle produced an entirely different present.
questions.explanation: The answer must state the changed outcome and at least two consequences, plus why a historian can read them.

questions.prompt: Why does the incident of the presidential chair matter to the story?
questions.answer: The chair matters because it converts the professor’s abstract displacement into a social fact. At a public meeting the seat of the president carries authority, and by trying to take it he claims a standing that exists only in his own world’s version of events; the crowd’s refusal to grant it, and their ejection of him, demonstrate that in that history his knowledge has no authority and his person no rank. The scene is comic — a man claiming a chair — and pointed, because it is the moment he stops observing the alternate world and tries to enter its public life and is refused. It also balances the story’s documentary evidence: the torn page shows the record is different, and the chair shows the society is different, and together they establish that the divergence runs through both things written and things lived.
questions.explanation: Three functions are required: authority denied, comedy converted into the personal stake, and the pairing with the torn page.

questions.prompt: How does the story use history as its material for science fiction? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The story’s science fiction is built entirely from historical material rather than from technology: there is no machine, no portal and no laboratory — only a historian, a battle and a city. Its premise takes the hinge-event of eighteenth-century Indian history, the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761, and alters a single outcome (Vishwasrao’s survival), after which every element of the present follows causally from that change: different political arrangements, different civic institutions, a different standing for different people. The protagonist’s expertise is essential to the genre mechanics, because only a Maratha-period historian can read the altered scenery as a chain of consequences rather than as decoration, and his specialist knowledge doubles as the reader’s guide. The story then gathers evidence in the classic detective pattern — the vacant chair demonstrating that his social standing belongs elsewhere, the torn page supplying a documented absence — so that the fantastic premise accumulates verification the way a mystery accumulates clues. Finally Rajendra Deshpande supplies the theoretical frame, invoking catastrophe theory and quantum ideas to argue that systems, and perhaps histories, can branch at critical thresholds, which converts the journey into a hypothesis the reader is invited to entertain rather than a dream to be dismissed. The story’s contribution to the genre is therefore epistemological rather than technological: it asks what makes a past real — the events, the record of them, or the authority that accepts the record — and uses the apparatus of science fiction to stage that question. Answers should trace premise, evidence and explanation in order with quotations, and note that the story deliberately leaves its science as an attractive framework within fiction.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the three layers traced with textual evidence, the observation that no technology drives the plot, and a judgement about the epistemological question the story stages.

questions.prompt: Is the story arguing that history is inevitable, or that it might have gone otherwise? Discuss.
questions.answer: The case for inevitability appears in the story only as the assumption it dismantles. The professor begins as a man of conventional historical training, for whom the defeat at Panipat is a fixed fact with fixed consequences, and his discomfort throughout the journey is the discomfort of someone whose professional certainty has been removed. Nothing in the alternate world is presented as miraculous: its institutions are ordinary, its citizens unpuzzled by their own present, and the difference traces back through ordinary causation to a single battle. If history were inevitable, the story implies, this world could not feel so normal to the people inside it — and the ease with which the alternate India conducts its affairs is itself the argument against necessity. The case for contingency, then, is carried by the design of the entire premise. One altered outcome — Vishwasrao surviving — produces a different political India, and because the change is small while the consequences are civilisational, the story demonstrates that hinge-events are not foreordained. Deshpande’s scientific frame reinforces this: catastrophe theory describes systems that sit stable until a small input flips them, and the quantum suggestion about branching extends the same idea from states to histories. The torn page adds a documentary dimension — the divergence is written into the record of that world, which means contingency has left an archive, not merely a dream. A subtler counter-argument deserves note: the professor cannot alter the alternate world, and he is ejected from it, which suggests that any single history, once lived, is fixed for those inside it — contingency may belong to the past as a whole but not to any individual present. The balanced judgement is that the story argues contingency at the level of the past and inevitability at the level of experience: any of several histories might have obtained, but whichever obtains becomes solid, documented and resistant to the people who live in it. Answers should support both readings with the premise, the science and the chair, and end with that distinction, because it is what separates the story’s cleverness from a simple claim that anything could have happened.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both readings evidenced, the distinction between contingency of the past and fixity of any present, and a judgement drawn from the story’s structure rather than its science alone.
